page_lead: This page summarizes common childbirth practices and typical hospital expectations in Japan using titles and details.

item_01.title: The belly band custom on the Day of the Dog
item_01.detail: In Japan, some families visit a shrine to pray for a safe birth. Around the fifth month of pregnancy, they may go on an auspicious “Day of the Dog” or on another convenient day. Some people also wear a belly band, called haraobi, because dogs are associated with many births and relatively easy delivery. This is done with wishes such as “May the baby be born healthy” and “May the birth be safe.” Some shrines give belly bands with a dog mark. A belly band may also be used to support the abdomen. It is not required, but some people value it as part of Japanese culture.

item_02.title: Typical number of prenatal checkups
item_02.detail: Once you know you are pregnant, visit a hospital or clinic as early as possible. The hospital checks whether you are pregnant and whether the baby is growing inside the uterus. During pregnancy, regular prenatal checkups are important for checking the health of the mother and baby. In Japan, many people visit the hospital about 14 times before birth. A common schedule is once every 4 weeks until 23 weeks, once every 2 weeks from 24 to 35 weeks, and once a week from 36 weeks until birth. The number of visits may increase depending on the mother’s or baby’s condition. At prenatal checkups, staff check weight, blood pressure, urine, the baby’s size, and the baby’s condition. You can ask doctors or midwives about any worries or questions.

item_03.title: Subsidies available through coupons
item_03.detail: Many municipalities give prenatal checkup tickets or coupons. By using them, part of the checkup cost can be supported. The number of tickets, amount of support, and how to use them differ by municipality. Please ask your municipal office or hospital for details.

item_04.title: Preparing for hospitalization: what to bring
item_04.detail: You will need items such as the Maternal and Child Health Handbook, health insurance card, patient registration card, changes of clothes, and clothes for the baby to wear when leaving the hospital. Required items differ by hospital. Clothes worn by the mother after birth, such as pajamas, may be rented from the hospital or may need to be brought from home. Check the packing list provided by the hospital.

item_05.title: Common delivery methods in Japan
item_05.detail: In Japan, several delivery methods may be used depending on the mother’s and baby’s condition, the course of pregnancy, and the mother’s wishes. Vaginal delivery is the most common method, where the baby is born through the birth canal. Natural delivery aims to keep medical intervention as low as possible while following the progress of labor. Epidural delivery uses anesthesia to reduce labor pain, although pain may not disappear completely. Facilities that provide epidural delivery are limited in Japan and often require advance reservation. Induced or planned delivery uses medicine to start or strengthen labor when medically needed for safety. Cesarean section is surgery to deliver the baby. In Japan it is chosen when medically necessary, and elective cesarean by personal request is generally not available. Planned cesarean may be used for breech position, multiple pregnancy, or previous cesarean birth. Emergency cesarean is used when the mother or baby is judged to be in danger during labor. Other methods include vacuum or forceps delivery when help is needed, water birth at limited facilities, and free-style birth in positions such as hands-and-knees or sitting.

item_06.title: What to confirm if you want epidural delivery
item_06.detail: Hospitals that provide epidural delivery are limited, and advance reservation is often needed. If you want this option, consult medical staff from early pregnancy. Even at facilities that offer epidural delivery, available days and times differ. Because of anesthesiologist schedules and other staffing issues, some hospitals cannot provide it 24 hours a day, at night, or on weekends. Confirm the details in advance.

item_07.title: Who can attend the birth and possible restrictions
item_07.detail: Birth attendance means that family members or others stay near the mother during childbirth. Who can attend depends on the hospital. Often it is a partner or family member, but some hospitals do not allow children, limit the number of people, or set time restrictions. Attendance may also be unavailable because of infection control or other rules. Check the hospital’s policy in advance.

item_08.title: How to travel to the hospital when labor begins
item_08.detail: Some hospitals ask pregnant people not to drive themselves when labor begins because stronger contractions can make safe driving difficult. In some areas, labor taxi services are available. Check your route to the hospital in advance so that you can travel safely. Because the progress of birth is unpredictable, avoid using public transportation when possible.

item_09.title: Photography during childbirth
item_09.detail: Nurses may sometimes help take photos during childbirth. However, some facilities prohibit photos or videos. If you have requests, check the hospital rules and birth attendance conditions in advance.

item_10.title: Typical length of hospital stay
item_10.detail: For vaginal delivery, many hospitals guide first-time mothers to stay around 5 days and mothers who have given birth before to stay around 3 to 5 days. After cesarean section, the hospital stay is generally about 7 to 10 days on average, which is a little longer than vaginal delivery. The length may change depending on the mother’s condition, the baby’s condition, and hospital policy.

item_11.title: Room choices and manners during hospitalization
item_11.detail: During hospitalization, you may be able to choose a shared room or a private room. A private room may cost extra, and it may not always be available even if requested. In Japanese hospitals, it is important to stay quiet so everyone can rest. In shared rooms, speak softly. Use earphones when watching television or videos. Use the visiting area when talking on the phone, when there are many visitors, or when conversations will be long.

item_12.title: Guidance often received during hospitalization
item_12.detail: During the hospital stay, many people receive guidance on breastfeeding and how to bathe the baby. The content and number of sessions differ by hospital, but explanations are commonly provided so that families can care for the baby with more confidence after discharge.

item_13.title: The role of nurses
item_13.detail: Nurses are professionals who provide medical care and nursing care. They are not people who do every personal task instead of the patient. You can consult them if you have trouble, but what they can do depends on the hospital system.

item_14.title: Restrictions on visiting hours and number of visitors
item_14.detail: Hospitals have rules about visiting hours and the number of visitors. For infection prevention and other reasons, visits by children may be restricted. Rules differ by hospital, so it is important to check in advance.

item_15.title: The custom of taking the umbilical cord home
item_15.detail: In Japan, there is a custom of taking the baby’s umbilical cord home as a keepsake. Some hospitals give it in a small box. How this is handled differs by hospital.

item_16.title: Religious considerations and meal support
item_16.detail: If there are foods you cannot eat for religious reasons, the support available differs by hospital. Many hospitals can provide meals for allergies, but some cannot provide meals that match religious dietary rules. If you have requests, consult the hospital in advance.

item_17.title: Examinations and interviews after childbirth during hospitalization
item_17.detail: After childbirth, daily rounds or examinations are common during hospitalization. Doctors or nurses may also ask questions to check your physical condition.

item_18.title: Where to submit the birth registration
item_18.detail: The birth registration must be submitted to the city, ward, town, or village office within 14 days after the baby is born. There is no municipal office counter inside the hospital, so prepare to go to the municipal office. In principle, the baby’s father or mother must submit it.

item_19.title: Use of a personal seal at admission
item_19.detail: Some hospitals require a personal seal, or hanko, for admission procedures. Recently, some hospitals do not use personal seals. Still, check the hospital’s list of things to bring carefully.

item_20.title: Newborn home visit
item_20.detail: A newborn home visit is a service where a municipal public health nurse or similar professional comes to your home after the baby is born. They can check the baby’s growth and condition and you can consult them about childcare.

item_21.title: About omiyamairi
item_21.detail: Omiyamairi is a traditional Japanese event to celebrate the baby’s birth at a shrine. Families visit a shrine and pray for the baby to grow well. It is often done around 31 days after birth for boys and around 33 days for girls, but the timing differs by family. Some families go later, prioritizing the mother’s and baby’s condition. On the day, the baby may wear special clothes and the family may take photos. Some families receive a shrine prayer, called gokito, asking for the baby’s healthy growth. It is not required, but many families do it as one part of Japanese culture.

item_22.title: About okuizome
item_22.detail: Okuizome is a traditional Japanese celebration held around 100 days after the baby is born. A special meal is prepared with the wish that the child will never have trouble finding food. The baby does not actually eat the meal yet and only pretends to eat. It is often held at home or at a restaurant, not at the hospital.

item_23.title: Postpartum checkups and infant checkups
item_23.detail: After birth, the mother usually has a one-month postpartum checkup. Some hospitals also have a two-week checkup. Municipalities may send information about infant checkups. Infant checkups are done to check growth and health. Common timing includes around one month at the hospital, and later around 3 to 4 months, 6 to 10 months, and around one year at the municipality. The number and timing differ by area.

item_24.title: Rules for riding in a car with a baby
item_24.detail: When putting a baby in a car, use a child seat that matches the baby’s age and body size. In Japan, children must use a child seat by law until they turn 6 years old.

item_25.title: Celebrations for a baby’s first birthday
item_25.detail: In Japan, some families celebrate when a baby turns 1 year old. One custom is issho-mochi, where the child carries about 2 kilograms of rice cake. It expresses the wish that the child will never have trouble with food throughout life. This is a traditional Japanese custom, but it is not required. Each family may do it differently.
